Compares fkYAML with yaml-cpp 0.9.0, libfyaml v1.0.0-beta1, and rapidyaml v0.16.0 (in-place and arena). corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ 11.4.0, CMake Release; tools/benchmark/CMakeLists.txt adds -O2 to the benchmarker target (which compiles header-only fkYAML); yaml-cpp/rapidyaml/libfyaml are built via FetchContent under their own Release flags
corrections.caveats: Numbers come from the project's own tool, but the tool's code, library versions, compiler and CPU are all public or stated. No third party has reproduced them yet. The runs are single Google Benchmark runs under WSL2. The ubuntu.yml result header reports 12 CPUs, while the other two runs report 16 CPUs from the same session. In the harness, the libfyaml loop never calls fy_document_destroy, so libfyaml's teardown is not timed; yaml-cpp and fkYAML nodes are destroyed inside the loop. This affects only the libfyaml comparison, not the yaml-cpp one.

notes: The benchmark_url given (tools/benchmark/README.md) has only usage instructions and no numbers. tier_reason: The fkYAML README Benchmarking tables have libfyaml rows at 35.9803/50.7076/21.9363 Mi/s against yaml-cpp at 10.122/16.6685/7.30883 Mi/s. The raw outputs are in fkYAML tools/benchmark/results. The benchmark code is public (fkYAML tools/benchmark/main.cpp and CMakeLists.txt pin libfyaml v1.0.0-beta1 and yaml-cpp 0.9.0 in a Release build; libfyaml's own CMakeLists adds -O2 for non-Debug builds). The compiler (g++ 11.4.0) and CPU (Ryzen 7 5800H) are stated, and third-party runs qualify for A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: g++ 11.4.0 (the only compiler the fkYAML README names; libfyaml's C sources use the configured C compiler), CMake Release; libfyaml is built as a static library via FetchContent, and its CMakeLists adds -O2 for non-Debug builds
corrections.workload: fkYAML's third-party Google Benchmark harness (tools/benchmark/main.cpp) calls fy_document_build_from_string with default config on in-memory ubuntu.yml, citm_catalog.json and citm_catalog.yml, reporting bytes/sec. It compares libfyaml v1.0.0-beta1 against yaml-cpp 0.9.0 (plus fkYAML and rapidyaml v0.16.0) on the same machine and build. Results were committed 2026-09-07, one run per file.
corrections.caveats: The benchmark was run by a third party (fkYAML's author, a competing library), not by libfyaml. libfyaml has no speed comparison of its own. The harness never calls fy_document_destroy inside the timed loop, so libfyaml's teardown is excluded while yaml-cpp's is timed. That slightly favors libfyaml, and the leaked documents also accumulate across iterations. libfyaml's opt-in transparent parse cache is not enabled with the default config used here. The runs are single Google Benchmark runs under WSL2, and no one has reproduced them independently. libfyaml is slower than both rapidyaml and fkYAML in this test.

notes: The comparison against yaml-cpp and all three derived ratios (~3.6x, ~3.0x, ~3.0x) check out. The benchmark_url was changed to the fkYAML README section that actually contains the numbers. last_commit was the pushed_at date; the newest commit on master is 2026-09-23.

tier_reason: The README 'C++ DOM throughput (x86-64, AVX2)' table gives Parshred FastDOM at 2572/2722/2519/1678/1317 MB/s and pugixml at 1465/821/1585/641/712 MB/s, measured on a stated Ryzen 5 7640U with GCC 16.1 -O3 (single thread). The benchmark code is public (bench/bench_dom.cpp, whose header gives the compile line g++ -std=c++20 -O3 -mavx2 against RapidXML 1.13 and pugixml 1.14). The library is built with the CMake release preset (-O3 -DNDEBUG).

corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 16.1, -O3 (README); bench/bench_dom.cpp header compile line: g++ -std=c++20 -O3 -mavx2; library built with the CMake 'release' preset (-O3 -DNDEBUG plus per-TU SIMD flags); single thread
corrections.workload: Single-threaded in-memory DOM parse of synthetic generated XML (repeated <item id name status>text</item> records under <root>) at 64 KB to 128 MB (bench/bench_dom.cpp, median of 50 down to 2 runs per size). Parshred runs fast_dom_parse<FDOM_FASTEST>, which skips text nodes and comments. It is compared with RapidXML 1.13 parse_fastest (also skips data nodes) and pugixml 1.14 load_buffer with parse_minimal (copies the input and still builds PCDATA nodes).
corrections.caveats: This is a first-party benchmark, but the code, compiler, flags and CPU are all public or stated. No third party has reproduced it yet. The workload is one synthetic, homogeneous XML shape, not real-world files. The pugixml comparison is not like for like. Parshred's FDOM_FASTEST mode skips text nodes, while pugixml builds PCDATA nodes and load_buffer copies the input (load_buffer_inplace would not). The pugixml ratios (1.6x to 3.3x) therefore overstate a same-work comparison somewhat. bench_dom.cpp is not part of the CMake build; it is compiled by hand. docs/performance.md still shows older approximate numbers on unnamed hardware (1.3-1.5x vs RapidXML, 2-2.5x vs pugixml) that contradict the README. The license is AGPL-3.0-or-later (strong network copyleft), with a paid commercial license on offer. The project is very new (created 2026-07-11) and has 0 stars.

notes: All README numbers and the derived pugixml ratios check out, as does the RapidXML statement (within ~5% up to 16 MB, 1.52-1.83x at 64 MB and above, and 'up to 2.4x' on other machines). The DOM_FASTEST in-situ run earlier in bench_dom does not mutate the shared buffer (make_insitu_sv writes nothing), so the later RapidXML and pugixml runs are not affected. The license was tightened to AGPL-3.0-or-later per the README and pyproject; it is OSI-approved, so usability stays copyable.
